text: On Linux, CLOCK_REALTIME (wall-clock time) is affected by discontinuous jumps, e.g. when NTP or an admin steps the clock; CLOCK_MONOTONIC is not, but it does not tell wall time. Time-based ID generators therefore detect a backwards step and wait or refuse, as Twitter's Snowflake does.
why: Shows the safe way to handle the clock-going-back case the item rules out.

text: ntpd slews the clock only when the offset is under 128 ms and steps it when the offset is larger. Kernel slewing is limited to 0.5 ms per second, so each second of correction takes about 2000 s to apply.
why: Explains when the clock slows down and when it jumps.

text: A write() normally lands in the OS page cache. Only fsync() flushes the file's modified data to the storage device, so it can be read back after a crash or reboot. That flush is the expensive part of 'save the counter on every ID'.
why: Clarifies what 'saving to disk' must mean to survive a crash.

text: RFC 9562 (May 2024) says UUID versions that are not time-ordered, such as UUIDv4, 'have poor database-index locality'. It introduced UUIDv7, a time-ordered UUID built on the Unix-epoch millisecond timestamp, to fix this.
why: Updates the 'UUIDs index badly' point with the current standard.

text: PostgreSQL 18 provides uuidv7(), which generates a time-ordered UUID from a millisecond Unix timestamp plus a sub-millisecond part and random bits, alongside gen_random_uuid()/uuidv4() for random UUIDs.
why: Shows time-ordered UUIDs are now built into a major database.

text: In InnoDB, every secondary-index record contains the row's primary-key columns. MySQL's manual notes that a long primary key makes all secondary indexes use more space, so a short primary key is advantageous.
why: Explains why a 16-byte key costs more than the primary index alone.

text: OWASP recommends replacing enumerable numeric identifiers with random ones like GUIDs, but stresses that 'even with complex identifiers, access control checks are essential'.
why: Stops readers treating unguessable IDs as security.

text: MongoDB's ObjectId timestamp has one-second resolution. The 5-byte random value is generated once per client process, and the 3-byte counter starts at a random value. Timestamp and counter are stored big-endian, so ObjectIds sort roughly by creation second.
why: Corrects the 'epoch milliseconds' impression and explains ObjectId ordering.

text: Flickr's published query is REPLACE INTO Tickets64 (stub) VALUES ('a'); followed by SELECT LAST_INSERT_ID();. REPLACE removes and reinserts the single 'a' row, so the auto-increment counter hands out the next value.
why: Gives readers the exact working query.

text: Flickr reports its two ticket servers drift out of sync - at the time of writing it had a few hundred thousand more odd-numbered objects than even-numbered ones - 'but this hurts no one'.
why: Real-world confirmation that the odd/even split is only roughly ordered.

text: Flickr deliberately does not replicate between its two ticket servers: at that write volume 'replicating between the boxes would be problematic, and locking would kill the performance of the site'.
why: Shows why the design avoids coordination.

text: When MySQL Group Replication runs in multi-primary mode and the variables are at their defaults, it sets auto_increment_increment to 7 and auto_increment_offset to the server ID, so each primary generates non-colliding auto-increment values.
why: Shows MySQL's built-in answer to multi-master auto-increment collisions.

text: InnoDB auto-increment values are never reused after a rollback, so gaps are normal. Under the default interleaved lock mode, values from concurrently running INSERT statements are interleaved.
why: Explains why even a single MySQL server does not give gap-free IDs.

text: InnoDB writes the current maximum auto-increment counter to the redo log and data dictionary, so the counter survives server restarts and a restarted ticket server resumes where it stopped.
why: Backs the 'resumes where it left off' claim.

text: Twitter's 2010 Snowflake was a Thrift server written in Scala. Twitter has retired that open-source release (repository archived in September 2021); the internal version is described as a full rewrite on Twitter's infrastructure.
why: Gives the accurate history of how Snowflake was deployed.

text: Twitter's stated Snowflake requirements were 'minimum 10k ids per second per process' with a response time of about 2 ms plus network latency, IDs under 64 bits, and k-sorted ordering.
why: Shows the actual design targets behind the bit layout.

text: Snowflake promised IDs 'k-sorted' within one second, aiming for tens of milliseconds, rather than strictly ordered.
why: Quantifies 'almost ordered'.

text: Discord documents its snowflake as a 42-bit timestamp (bits 63-22, milliseconds since 2015-01-01), a 5-bit internal worker ID, a 5-bit process ID and a 12-bit increment. Its HTTP API returns these IDs as strings.
why: Shows the machine-ID bits can be split further and why IDs are sent as strings.

text: Sonyflake trades per-instance throughput for lifetime and machine count: 39 bits of time in 10 ms units (about 174 years), an 8-bit sequence (256 IDs per 10 ms) and a 16-bit machine ID (65,536 machines).
why: Shows how changing the bit split changes the limits.

text: Google Spanner's TrueTime lets it assign monotonically increasing commit timestamps across all servers without global communication, so transactions appear in a serial order consistent with commit order.
why: Counter-example showing strict global ordering is possible with special infrastructure.

text: TiDB's Placement Driver allocates timestamps (TSO) that always move forward: 46 bits of physical milliseconds plus an 18-bit logical counter for multiple timestamps within the same millisecond.
why: A practical high-throughput monotonic timestamp service.

text: Amazon SQS standard queues are at-least-once: a message copy can occasionally be delivered again, and AWS tells applications to be idempotent. If ID ranges are distributed through such a queue, a redelivered range would produce duplicate IDs unless consumers deduplicate.
why: Flags a real correctness risk in the queue-based variant.

text: DynamoDB's UpdateItem can act as an atomic counter, but the update is not idempotent: a retried increment can overcount. For range allocation that only wastes a range, which is safe.
why: Shows why atomic-increment stores are a safe range source.

text: Meituan's open-source Leaf ID service offers both models from this lecture: a database-backed 'segment' (range) mode and a snowflake mode taken from Twitter's algorithm, which needs a ZooKeeper address.
why: Points readers to a production implementation of the batched-range design.

text: A common 32.768 kHz tuning-fork crystal is typically accurate to about +/-20 ppm at room temperature. Its error follows a parabolic curve with a coefficient of about 0.04 ppm/C^2, so accuracy drops at both high and low temperature extremes.
why: Gives the real temperature behaviour behind clock drift.
